issues.item: Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Night' implies fear linked to darkness/outdoor danger, but there are no Threat items and no memory/trigger content tied to night-time, darkness, or outdoor contexts. For this relief-worker trauma, that strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is the least coherent item because it addresses a threat context not otherwise represented across Triggers, Memory, or Negative Appraisals.

Yet the selected Threat items are central, high-intensity PTSD threat responses and are also mirrored elsewhere. This makes Threat functionally active in a way that contradicts the formulation structure.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Entrapment could occur, but here it lacks a clear connection to the rest of the selected content and weakens coherence.

However, the selected threat items describe an active symptomatic threat response cluster (strong emotional/physical reactivity and concentration disruption) that appears tightly tied to triggers and memory intrusions. This creates a contradiction with the formulation structure, especially given concurrent trigger and memory items that imply exactly the kind of reminder-linked threat activation the model marks as inactive. The other nodes are broadly coherent with each other and with the trauma type.

Threat has no active incoming or outgoing edges, so it should not appear as a tightly integrated maintaining component. Yet all three selected Threat items are non-specific PTSD symptom/severity indicators rather than a coherent sense of current threat, and they are not meaningfully linked to the active Triggers, Memory, Negative Appraisals, and Maladaptive Strategies pattern.

Threat is structurally isolated in the formulation, but 'Scanning for Danger' is tightly mirrored by both Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings' and Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time,' making threat function as an active linked node rather than an isolated one.

Negative Appraisals: 'I have to be on guard all the time' overlaps almost exactly with Threat: 'Scanning for Danger' and Maladaptive Strategies: 'Checking Surroundings,' which contradicts the formulation because Threat has no active links to or from these nodes.

vignette: Kiet Truong's eyes still scan the room with a practiced intensity, a habit formed during his years as a relief worker in war-torn countries. It's been decades since he last navigated the treacherous terrain of a conflict zone, but the memories remain, etched into his mind like scars on a well-worn map. As an 80-year-old widower and retired data scientist, Kiet should be enjoying a quiet life, surrounded by the comforts of routine and familiarity. Instead, he finds himself constantly on edge, as if waiting for the other shoe to drop. It started after a particularly harrowing incident in his final deployment. His team had been caught in a skirmish between rival factions, and they were forced to flee under heavy fire. Kiet remembers feeling trapped, with no options but to keep moving forward, praying that they would make it out alive. Even now, when he's surrounded by the peaceful silence of his home, those feelings of entrapment can resurface at a moment's notice. Kiet has learned to avoid news reports about conflicts or natural disasters, unable to bear the sight of others suffering in ways that echo his own experiences. He'll quickly change the channel or shut off the radio, but the images linger, seeping into his dreams and leaving him feeling shaken and disoriented upon waking. These nightmares are particularly distressing because they feel so real - as if he's reliving the event all over again. To cope with these feelings of anxiety, Kiet has developed a few strategies that bring him some fleeting sense of control. He'll rehearse conversations before meeting with friends or family, trying to anticipate every possible topic and preparing responses in advance. It's exhausting, but it helps him feel more grounded, less likely to be caught off guard by an unexpected question or comment. When he's out in public, Kiet constantly scans his surroundings, searching for signs of potential threats. He knows it's irrational - he's not in a war zone anymore - but the habit persists, fueled by his deep-seated fear that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place. This hypervigilance takes a toll on his relationships; friends and family have begun to notice his distant behavior, his reluctance to engage in conversations or activities. Despite these efforts to cope, Kiet can't shake the feeling that he's losing his grip on reality. He worries that his reactions to these triggers mean he's going crazy, that the trauma has finally caught up with him after all these years. The memories of that event continue to replay in his mind like a film loop, each iteration reinforcing his fear that he'll never be able to escape the past. Lately, Kiet has become increasingly irritable, snapping at those around him for no reason. He's mortified by these outbursts, convinced that they're proof of his own instability. His body feels constantly tense, as if waiting for the next blow - a physical manifestation of the emotional turmoil brewing inside. It was one particularly brutal nightmare, followed by a morning of unshakeable anxiety, that finally brought Kiet to seek help. As he sat in his armchair, feeling like he was drowning in a sea of fear and uncertainty, he realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He wants to learn how to quiet the constant threat monitoring, to find some measure of peace in a world that still feels treacherous. For Kiet Truong, the journey ahead will be long and difficult, but with support, he hopes to finally begin healing - and finding his way back to a life free from the grip of trauma.
